title: Sunny Liang Tan
text:
I grew up in Hunan and moved to Hong Kong for university, where I earned my bachelor’s degree in Economics and Finance at the University of Hong Kong in 2019. I then continued my education in the United States, completing a master’s degree in Economics at Duke University in 2021 before beginning my Ph.D. at UCLA. I was a visiting scholar in the MIT Department of Economics in 2024–2025.
I enjoy traveling and learning about economies firsthand. My research trips have taken me to Mexico, Spain, and Vietnam.

title: Research
text: Industrial policy can reshape production well beyond the firms it directly supports, and assessing its aggregate productivity implications therefore requires measuring how supply-chain spillovers amplify or counteract recipient gains. This paper provides the first joint analysis of these direct, upstream, and downstream contributions in the setting of government venture capital in China. Linking investment records to firm accounts, patents, and supplier–buyer transactions, we identify expansion among financed firms and their existing trading partners. Suppliers expand sales and capital, while buyers expand sales and payroll. We combine these responses with baseline allocation statistics in a production-network framework that values both the resources absorbed by expanding firms and those released elsewhere. In a broad-population calibration with fixed industry factor supplies, supplier and buyer spillovers amplify the recipient contribution, with the buyer contribution accounting for most of the total. Positive labor-reallocation contributions outweigh the negative capital-reallocation contributions at trading partners. The analysis shows that production networks can substantially enlarge the productivity contribution suggested by recipient outcomes alone, highlighting their importance for evaluating industrial policy.

title: Research
text:
Working Papers


Exchange-Rate Movements and U.S. Corporations

Joint with Ivo Welch and Yuqing Zhou.

This paper revisits the exchange-rate exposure puzzle: why prior research finds weak relationships between currency movements and U.S. firms’ stock returns despite substantial international trade. Linking transaction-level U.S. Census export records to financial statements and stock returns for publicly traded U.S. exporters from 1992 to 2016, we construct firm-specific exchange-rate exposure measures that reflect each firm’s export destinations. Dollar depreciation is associated with economically significant increases in exports, sales, profitability, and stock returns, with export, sales, and stock-return sensitivities generally larger among larger and more export-oriented firms. In asset- or export-weighted specifications, a 1% depreciation is associated with approximately 0.4-0.6% higher exports and 0.6-0.8% higher sales. The stronger sales response is consistent with currency movements affecting domestic competitiveness as well as foreign demand, while the profitability results indicate that financial and operational hedging do not fully offset exposure. Real operating sensitivities increase over time. Stock prices respond contemporaneously, with no detectable delayed response around subsequent earnings announcements. By measuring exposure using firms’ actual trading relationships and tracing its implications across operating outcomes and equity valuations, the paper contributes new evidence to the exchange-rate exposure literature and shows that substantial corporate currency exposure can coexist with timely incorporation of information into stock prices.

title: Research
text:
Work in Progress


Industrial Policy and Scale Complementarities in EV Battery Supply Chains

Joint with Binkai Chen and Junjie Xia.

I study whether automakers’ investments become more profitable when other automakers invest and buy from the same battery supplier. I exploit China’s 2020 EV subsidy reform, which raised the minimum qualifying driving range to 300 km, and compare models whose pre-reform certified ranges fell just above and below the cutoff. Using pre-reform sourcing links, I estimate how the eligibility cutoff affected the battery volumes supplied by each supplier. I then test whether those suppliers offered lower battery prices to their other automaker customers and whether those customers invested more than comparable automakers with similar subsidy exposure that sourced elsewhere. I use these estimates in a model with fixed costs in battery production to assess whether the gains from shared scale are large enough to make projects viable when automakers invest together.




Industrial Policy and Induced Innovation in Semiconductor Supply Chains

Joint with Mervyn Ho.

This paper studies whether industrial policy induces technological upgrading among semiconductor equipment makers by supporting their downstream customers. Chipmakers’ adoption of more advanced production technologies raises the technical requirements facing equipment suppliers. The resulting demand can make costly equipment development worthwhile, while repeated production, testing, and customer feedback can generate learning that benefits subsequent customers. Combining government venture capital investment records, administrative firm data, and supplier-buyer transactions with semiconductor fabrication capacity and process-technology data, the project traces equipment makers’ exposure to policy-supported chipmakers through pre-existing supply relationships. The empirical analysis distinguishes customer capacity expansion from advances in process technology and examines whether these changes induce corresponding capability upgrading among equipment suppliers. It investigates whether supplier upgrading varies with the duration and intensity of exposure to technologically advancing customers. The broader question is whether industrial policy can build technological capabilities across the semiconductor industry by inducing supplier innovations that benefit chipmakers beyond those it directly supports.




Multinational Investment and Regional Growth in Mexico

With Martin Tobal.

How does foreign investment translate into productive capabilities in a host economy? This paper develops an empirical framework for studying Chinese multinational investment in Mexico following the U.S.-China trade war. The central hypothesis is that foreign entry can generate persistent regional gains through worker learning, improved labor-market matching, and spillovers to domestic firms. These mechanisms must be distinguished from the direct increase in Mexican export demand caused by U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods. We propose linking employer-employee records, manufacturing establishment surveys, foreign-ownership information, and trade data to estimate regional responses and trace workers across foreign and domestic employers. The regional design combines predetermined employment shares with sectoral Chinese investment in Vietnam as a candidate instrument for Mexican investment. Worker-mobility analysis would separate employer wage premia from earnings gains that persist after foreign-firm experience. A quantitative spatial framework would connect these responses to migration, local prices, and welfare.




Chinese Multinationals’ Overseas Production and U.S. Sales
Using transaction-level U.S. import records from LFTTD, this project measures how Chinese multinationals’ production abroad supplies the U.S. market. It proposes linking foreign supplier identifiers to historical ownership data from Orbis and supplementary shipment records to identify Chinese-controlled manufacturing affiliates outside China. The analysis will trace these affiliates’ U.S.-bound shipments by product, country of origin, and U.S. buyer and estimate their share of U.S. imports. By separating overseas production under Chinese ownership from direct exports from China, it will measure Chinese firms’ role in supplying the United States through global production networks.
